title: Secure Code Review
summary: The security-specific lens a reviewer adds on top of a normal code review, focused on catching missing checks rather than style.

slides.markdown:
A normal code review asks: does this work, is it readable, is it tested. A **security-focused review** asks a different question on top of that: **what's missing that an attacker would notice, even though the code does exactly what it was written to do.**

That framing matters because most security bugs a review catches aren't wrong code — they're *absent* code: a missing authorization check, input that was never validated, an error path nobody thought about. This topic is about training the specific habit of looking for absence, which functional review (does the happy path work?) doesn't naturally develop.

slides.subTitle: Beyond a normal code review
slides.markdown:
A normal review is largely about **what the code does**: is the logic correct, are edge cases handled, is it readable and tested, does it follow team conventions. A security-focused pass layers on a different question: **what could this code let someone do that it shouldn't** — and, just as often, **what did this code assume that isn't actually guaranteed**.

The key mental shift is from reviewing the **happy path** to reviewing the **trust boundaries** the change touches: does new endpoint code check that the caller is authorized for this specific resource, not just authenticated in general? Does new input get validated before use, given the discipline from earlier in this group? Does an error path fail safely? A change can pass every functional review criterion — correct, tested, clean — and still introduce a serious vulnerability, because functional correctness and security correctness are checking genuinely different properties.

slides.subTitle: Authorization, input validation, secrets, error handling
slides.markdown:
A concrete, reusable set of questions to run against any change that touches user input, data access, or a new endpoint — not exhaustive, but catches a large share of real findings:

- **Authorization** — does every new or modified endpoint check that the caller is allowed to act on *this specific resource*, not just that they're logged in at all?
- **Input validation** — is every new input validated at the boundary it enters, following allowlist-first discipline?
- **Secrets** — does the diff introduce any hardcoded credential, API key, or token, even in a test file or a comment?
- **Error handling** — does a new error path leak internal detail to the caller, and does any new security-relevant check fail safe rather than fail open on an unexpected exception?

Running this checklist explicitly, every time, is what separates a security-focused review from "I'll notice if something looks obviously wrong" — most real findings aren't obviously wrong on a casual read, they're a specific missing check that only surfaces when you deliberately ask the specific question.

slides.sectionTitle: Spotting a missing authorization check in a diff
When a change needs a threat-model note
slides.subTitle: Vs when that's overkill
slides.markdown:
Not every change needs a formal threat-modeling exercise, and treating every pull request that way would make security review a bottleneck no team tolerates for long. A useful rule of thumb: a change needs an explicit threat-model note (a short written statement of what's being trusted, from whom, and why that's acceptable) when it **introduces a new trust boundary** — a new authentication mechanism, a new way external data enters the system, a new integration with a third party, a change to how authorization decisions get made.

A change that stays inside an existing, already-reviewed trust boundary — a new field on an existing, already-authorized endpoint, a UI-only change, a refactor with no behavior change — usually doesn't need one; the existing review checklist covers it fine. The judgment call is real and worth naming explicitly in review comments ("this touches auth logic, let's get a security review before merging" vs. "this is a display-only change, standard review is enough") rather than either skipping the question entirely or defaulting every change to the heavyweight process.

slides.sectionTitle: Numbers: how much of secure review is about absence
slides.markdown:
Analyses of real-world vulnerability findings consistently show that a large share — broken access control and injection-style issues have topped industry vulnerability lists for years — trace back to a missing check rather than an incorrect one: a validation that was never added, an authorization check that was never written, an error path nobody handled. Comparatively few findings come from a check that exists but has an outright logic bug.

This has a direct implication for how review time should be spent: scrutinizing the correctness of an *existing* check (is this comparison right, is this condition inverted) is valuable but addresses a smaller slice of real risk than asking "is there a check here at all" for the security-relevant properties a change touches. A reviewer optimizing for the highest-yield use of limited review time should weight toward actively looking for absence — the checklist habit — over line-by-line scrutiny of logic that's already present.

slides.sectionTitle: Reviewing for what the diff doesn't show
slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
The hardest and most senior-level part of secure code review isn't checking the lines that changed — it's reasoning about what the change **doesn't show**, because a diff view is inherently a partial picture. A new endpoint's authorization check might look correct in isolation but interact badly with an existing check somewhere else in the codebase that the diff doesn't touch — two independently-reasonable-looking pieces of authorization logic that, combined, leave a gap neither author individually introduced.

A senior reviewer specifically asks: does this change interact with any *existing* trust decision elsewhere in the system, not just "is this new code correct on its own terms"? Concretely: does a new bulk-export endpoint interact with an existing per-record authorization check that was written assuming single-record access, in a way that now bypasses it at scale? Does a new caching layer accidentally serve one user's authorized response to a different, unauthorized user because the cache key didn't account for identity?

This kind of review requires holding a mental model of the broader system, not just the diff in front of you — which is exactly why pairing an experienced-with-the-system reviewer alongside a security-checklist pass catches more than either alone, and why "this diff looks fine in isolation" is a weaker signal than it feels like during a fast-moving review.

slides.sectionTitle: Making the checklist structural, not just habitual
slides.markdown:
A checklist that lives only in an experienced reviewer's head has an obvious scaling problem: it depends on that specific person reviewing that specific PR, on a good day, remembering to apply it. The stronger version of secure code review, consistent with the platform-level enforcement theme running through this whole area, makes the checklist **structural**: a PR template with explicit security checkboxes ("does this change add or modify an authorization check? has it been reviewed by someone other than the author?"), a required reviewer group for any diff touching auth-related file paths, or an automated linter/SAST check that flags a new endpoint definition with no visible authorization decorator nearby.

None of these replace human judgment entirely — a linter can't reason about whether an authorization check is *correct* for the business logic, only whether one exists syntactically — but they convert "a thoughtful reviewer might catch this" into "the process requires someone to explicitly answer this question before merge," which is a meaningfully more reliable floor than relying on any individual reviewer's attention on a given day.

slides.sectionTitle: Reviewing only the changed lines and missing a bypass
slides.markdown:
The pitfall: a reviewer looks only at the lines a diff actually changes — standard practice for reviewing *correctness*, since that's usually where a bug would be — and misses that the change, taken together with unchanged code elsewhere, opens a new path that bypasses an existing security control entirely.

A concrete shape this takes: an existing authorization check lives in a shared middleware that runs for all requests through a specific route pattern. A new endpoint is added that technically matches a *different* route pattern (perhaps for a legitimate reason — a new API version, a slightly different path structure) and therefore never passes through that middleware at all — the endpoint's own code has no security bug in it whatsoever, the diff reviews cleanly, and yet the resource it exposes is now reachable with no authorization check applied, because the check that used to cover "all requests" never actually covered this route.

The fix is a review habit, not a tooling fix alone: for any new endpoint or entry point, explicitly verify which existing security controls (middleware, filters, gateways) it actually passes through — don't assume a control that covers most similar code automatically covers this new addition too, and treat "this is a new route/entry point" as itself a prompt to check that question directly.
